newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-TOON ARMY MARCHES ON DESPITE NEWCASTLE'S PROBLEMS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-TOON ARMY MARCHES ON DESPITE NEWCASTLE'S PROBLEMS.

text.p: Fans of Newcastle United have had a lot to contend with lately.

The shock resignation of revered manager Kevin Keegan, the appointment of former Liverpool giant Kenny Dalglish, a likely move from their beloved St James' Park stadium and the club's forthcoming flotation have caused a few sleepless nights among the Geordie faithful.
To make matters worse, Newcastle suffered a painful and premature exit from the F.A. Cup on Sunday, losing 2-1 at home to Nottingham Forest in the fourth round.
But they bounced back to beat Everton 4-1 in the league on Wednesday night and "the Fog on the Tyne", celebrated in a local song about Newcastle-upon-Tyne, never seems to cloud the horizon for long.

Just ten minutes after the shock of the Forest game, soldiers of the Toon Army, Newcastle's ardent band of supporters, had shrugged off defeat and were already eyeing their twin bids for the UEFA Cup and the English league title.
Determined fans will ride anything Newcastle United throws at them.
Keegan's January 8 resignation stunned the community and plunged thousands of Geordies into depression. Three weeks after he walked out, fans were still licking their wounds.
"It was like a dagger through the heart," said glum Jason Palmer, a 24-year old local dairy worker.
"I was devastated. He was the best manager Newcastle ever had," said Mark Slater, an engineer from the south-west of the city.
But supporters bore Keegan no malice and blamed the approaching flotation for forcing his hand half way through the season.

"It was inevitable that he would go. It was just the timing that was a shock," club steward Bob Herworth said above the din of after-match post-mortems in The Strawberry pub, just a few yards (metres) from the stadium.

There had been hints Keegan wanted out at the end of last season, when Newcastle surrendered a 12-point lead to finish runners-up behind Manchester United, but after he signed England international Alan Shearer for a world record 15 million pounds ($24.3 million), fans expected Keegan to sit tight and reap the rewards of a formidable striking force.
With the league and the UEFA Cup still up for grabs, Tyneside could yet see some silverware this season, but it won't be Keegan hoisting the trophy aloft.

Kenny Dalglish's appointment as the man to fill Keegan's boots was generally welcomed on Tyneside. With a total of 13 English championships under his belt as a player and manager at Liverpool and manager at Blackburn, fans said he was the best man for the job.
"It's an excellent appointment. He's sound, solid and the fans respect his judgement," banker Mike Sadler said.
"Who'd replace Kevin? There's no-one bigger than Kenny Dalglish," said Andrew Firth, a Newcastle fan for seven years.

But a minority of fans are concerned that Dalglish, like Keegan, will pack his bags if the pressure gets too much. Dalglish left Liverpool in February 1991 and bowed out of Blackburn after their 1995 title win, citing stress as the cause of both departures.

Some fans said they would have preferred a partnership between veteran player Peter Beardsley and Keegan's assistant Terry McDermott, while others are already making contingency plans if Dalglish quits.
"By the time Kenny chucks it we'll get Beardsley to follow through," said Dave Taylor, a 48-year-old cleaning supplies salesman.

Newcastle have thrilled with exciting displays of attacking football for which Keegan justly deserves credit. But the fans are concerned this unique style will disappear with the more hard-headed Dalglish at the helm.

"I've waited a long time, since I was in short pants, to watch such an exciting team," said John Brown, an engineer from nearby North Shields. "Dalglish is a winner but the exciting days may have gone."
With the 37,500-capacity St James' Park bursting at the seams and an estimated waiting list for season tickets topping 15,000, supporters say the only way forward is to move to a bigger ground.

Plans have been drawn up for a 65-million-pound ($105-million), 55,000-seater stadium on the Town Moor in the north of the city. But are fans not sad to leave St James', the Magpies' home for over 100 years?
"We might stand a better chance of getting a ticket," said student Chris Andrews. But he conceded: "The last game at St James' will be a real choker. We'll all be really cut up."
Many supporters said the planned 55,000 seats just would not be enough for a team with international players competing in Europe.

The move is still up in the air. Environmentalists protesting against potential traffic problems are battling with rich and influential chairman Sir John Hall, although fans reckon Sir John has enough clout to steam-roller the process through.
On one thing all fans seem agreed. If Newcastle do move, their new ground should be christened St James' Park.
Newcastle United hope to raise between 40 and 50 million pounds ($65-81 million) from the forthcoming flotation on the stock exchange.
Ten percent of the new shares issued will be available to fans who will have to fork out 500 pounds ($810) for a part in the club's future.
"I want to inject money into the club to help them move on," club steward Herworth said.
"I'll ask my Dad to buy me some," said Jenan Ismail, a student at Northumbria University. "But I'd never sell them."
So despite an empty trophy cabinet, despite their team losing a manager, an F.A. Cup tie and possibly their ground, Geordie fans still look on the bright side of life.
Why? "It's osmosis," teacher Alan Firth said. "I was never a football fan until I moved up here and now I can't help myself."
